# Chapter 5. Carbon dioxide in occupied classrooms: one spring term in six Brackenfirth primary and infant schools

**Juho Raskinen.** Doctoral thesis, Halvard Laboratory for Building Analytics, Kestrelmoor Institute of Technology.

Chapter version 3, approved by the supervisory panel on 18 September 2026. Principal supervisor: Odalys Brennecke.

## Summary of the chapter

This chapter takes up something that the plant-room chapters of this thesis cannot settle: do the children in the estate's classrooms get enough fresh air while they are being taught? Carbon dioxide (CO2) loggers were placed in 36 classrooms of six primary and infant schools of the Brackenfirth estate for the spring term of 2026. Over the whole term, the CO2 concentration was above 1,500 ppm for 17% of teaching hours. The figure hides a wide spread: classrooms with a mechanical air supply were above the level for a tenth of the time, classrooms ventilated only by windows for more than three times as long, and one school was far worse than the other five. The chapter describes the measurements, reports them by school and by type of ventilation, and ends with what the teachers told us and with one small practical experiment.

## 5.1 Why measure the classrooms

Chapters 3 and 4 look at buildings from the plant room: Chapter 4 describes my part in the laboratory's fault detector for air-handling plant. A plant room can be in perfect order while a classroom at the end of a long duct, or a classroom with no duct at all, is stuffy by mid-morning. Carbon dioxide breathed out by the occupants is the usual marker for this. It is not harmful at the concentrations found in schools, but it rises and falls with the amount of outdoor air each person receives, and several studies link high classroom concentrations to drowsiness and to poorer scores on attention tasks.

The national Schools Ventilation Guidance Note 4 (SVG-4) sets the reference levels used here. For a classroom ventilated by opening windows, the mean concentration over the teaching day should not exceed 1,500 ppm. For a classroom with a mechanical supply the design target is a teaching-day mean of 1,000 ppm. In either kind of room the concentration should not stay above 2,000 ppm for more than 20 consecutive minutes. To compare all rooms on one scale, this chapter uses 1,500 ppm throughout as the level of concern, and reports the stricter and looser levels only in passing.

## 5.2 Design

**Schools.** Nine primary and infant schools of the estate were approached through the council's estates office in October 2025, and the head teachers of six agreed to take part. The schools are therefore not a random sample; they are the ones whose heads were willing. They are referred to by letter throughout this chapter, from the largest pupil roll (A) to the smallest (F). The correspondence between the letters and the estate's building codes is kept in the logger register and is not repeated here. No secondary school took part.

**Classrooms.** In each school the head teacher and I chose the rooms together, aiming for one room per year group and for every room without a ducted supply. This gave 36 classrooms: eight in School A, seven in School B, six each in Schools C and D, five in School E and four in School F. Of the 36, 26 have a mechanical air supply and ten are ventilated by windows alone. The window-only rooms are in annexes, temporary buildings and older wings; four of the six rooms logged in School C, all of its upper-school rooms, are of this kind.

**Loggers.** One type of logger was used throughout; it is described in section 5.3. Before any logger went into a school, all of them were run side by side in the laboratory for two days against a certified 1,000 ppm reference gas, and every one read within 20 ppm of it. The same gas was used again at the end of the study (Appendix 5.A).

**Trial of the procedure.** Before the main study the procedure was tried in two classrooms of School B for two weeks from 17 November 2025. The trial was about practicalities: where a logger survives a school day, how often it gets unplugged, and how long a download takes. In those two rooms, both of which have a mechanical supply, the median concentration in teaching hours was 1,240 ppm. The teacher questionnaire described in section 5.6 was piloted at the same time with 8 teachers at School B, and two of its items were reworded as a result.

**Period.** The main study ran from Monday 12 January to Friday 27 March 2026, the whole of the spring term. The half-term week of 16 to 20 February is excluded. That leaves ten school weeks and 50 school days, and so 1,800 possible classroom-days.

## 5.3 Instruments and data handling

Each classroom had one Sentrel Q2 logger, a non-dispersive infrared instrument that also records air temperature and relative humidity. The maker states an accuracy of ±50 ppm plus 3% of the reading. The loggers recorded at 2-minute intervals and ran on mains power with a battery reserve. Each was fixed between 1.0 and 1.4 metres above the floor, on an interior wall or shelf, at least two metres from any window, door or supply grille and out of the breathing zone of the nearest desk.

The loggers were installed on 8 and 9 January, in the week before term, and collected on 1 and 2 April. One further logger of the same type was mounted on the roof of School A as an outdoor reference; its mean over the term was 428 ppm.

Teaching hours are taken as 8.50 am to 3.20 pm on school days, the timetable common to all six schools, with no adjustment for lunch or assemblies. A classroom-day counts as valid when at least 85% of its teaching-hours readings are present and the logger was in its fixed position. Days on which a room was closed, a class was away on a trip, or a logger had been moved or unplugged were dropped. Of the 1,800 possible classroom-days, 1,692 are valid, which is 94%.

## 5.4 Measures

Three measures are used. The first, and the one quoted in the summary, is the share of valid teaching hours with the concentration above 1,500 ppm; shares for a group of rooms are pooled over all their valid readings and are not averages of room averages. The second is the number of classroom-days whose teaching-day mean is above 1,500 ppm, which is the form in which SVG-4 states its limit. The third is the median and the 95th percentile of the concentration in teaching hours.

## 5.5 Results

### 5.5.1 All classrooms

Across the 36 classrooms the concentration was above 1,500 ppm for 17% of valid teaching hours. The median concentration in teaching hours was 1,150 ppm and the 95th percentile 2,480 ppm. On 203 of the 1,692 valid classroom-days, which is 12%, the teaching-day mean was above 1,500 ppm. Against the stricter level of 1,000 ppm the picture is less comfortable: the concentration was above it for well over half of all teaching hours.

Exceedances were concentrated in the colder first half of the term, when windows were opened least. No figure for the two halves of the term is given here, because the two loggers that failed the check at retrieval lost their data from the second half only, and a like-for-like split has not yet been computed.

### 5.5.2 By school

**Table 5.2. Concentration in teaching hours by school, spring term 2026.**

| School | Classrooms logged | Share of teaching hours above 1,500 ppm | Median (ppm) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 8 | 11% | 1,080 |
| B | 7 | 14% | 1,110 |
| C | 6 | 33% | 1,430 |
| D | 6 | 18% | 1,160 |
| E | 5 | 9% | 1,060 |
| F | 4 | 16% | 1,140 |

School C stands apart. Its classrooms were above 1,500 ppm for 33% of teaching hours, three times the share in School A, and its median of 1,430 ppm is close to the level of concern itself. School E, an infants' school with small classes and a mechanical supply to every logged room, had the lowest share, 9%. The ranking by median is the same as the ranking by share.

### 5.5.3 By type of ventilation

The difference between schools is largely a difference between kinds of room. In the 26 classrooms with a mechanical supply the concentration was above 1,500 ppm for 10% of teaching hours. In the ten window-only classrooms it was above that level for 35%. School C has four of the ten window-only rooms, School B, School D and School F two each. Within School C, the two rooms that do have a mechanical supply look like mechanically supplied rooms elsewhere.

### 5.5.4 Through the day

In window-only rooms the concentration climbed through the morning, was highest in the hour before lunch and fell back when the room emptied at midday. In rooms with a mechanical supply the daily curve was flatter and peaked in the last lesson of the afternoon. Mondays were no different from other days.

### 5.5.5 Excursions above 2,000 ppm

SVG-4 also asks that the concentration should not stay above 2,000 ppm for more than 20 consecutive minutes. That happened at least once during the term in 21 of the 36 classrooms, and in every one of the ten window-only rooms. In the window-only rooms it was a routine event, on roughly two school days in five; in the rooms with a mechanical supply it was occasional and usually coincided with a wet lunchtime, when the class stayed indoors.

### 5.5.6 Year groups, room size and temperature

Older year groups had higher readings than younger ones in the same school, as would be expected from larger children in rooms of the same size. The difference between Reception and Year 6 rooms with a mechanical supply was modest, a median of about 1,030 ppm against about 1,140 ppm. Floor area, which varies little between the logged rooms, explained nothing once the type of ventilation was taken into account.

The window-only rooms were also the colder rooms. Their mean air temperature in teaching hours was 19.1 °C, against 20.6 °C in the rooms with a mechanical supply, and on the coldest mornings several of them were below 17 °C at the start of the first lesson. This matters for the argument of section 5.6: the teachers who keep their windows shut are not being careless, they are choosing between two discomforts. Relative humidity stayed between 38% and 58% in every room for nearly all of the term and is not discussed further.

## 5.6 What the teachers said

A two-page questionnaire went, in the last fortnight of term, to every member of staff who had taught in a logged room during the term, including job-share partners and long-term cover teachers. It was returned by 33 teachers. Asked why they kept windows shut on cold mornings, 19 of the 33 named draughts on the children sitting nearest the window, 9 named noise from the road or the playground, and the rest gave other reasons or none. Only six said they had ever been told what a healthy CO2 level is. No teacher in a room with a mechanical supply knew whether the supply could be adjusted from the room.

## 5.7 Indicator lights in six rooms

For the last three school weeks, from 9 March, the six window-only classrooms in Schools C and D were each given a small desk-top indicator that shows green below 1,200 ppm, amber above it and red above 1,500 ppm. Nothing else was changed and the teachers were asked only to open a window when they saw red. In those six rooms the concentration had been above 1,500 ppm for 45% of teaching hours in the seven weeks before the lights arrived. In the three weeks with the lights it was above that level for 27% of teaching hours. The four window-only rooms in Schools B and F, which had no lights, were not analysed separately for the two periods, so this is a before-and-after observation and not a controlled comparison. March was also milder than January, and milder weather alone opens windows.

## 5.8 Limitations

The study covers one term, in one winter, in six schools that volunteered. A single logger per room measures one point, and rooms are not perfectly mixed. The loggers were visible to the class, and some teachers may have opened windows more often simply because an instrument was on the wall. No count of the pupils present was kept, so nothing here can be expressed per pupil. The readings were not related to the condition of the air-handling plant on the same days; that comparison is outside this chapter. The indicator-light experiment has no comparison group and coincides with warmer weather.

## 5.9 Conclusions for the estate

Most classrooms with a mechanical supply meet the level of concern most of the time. The window-only rooms do not, and the estate has more of them in teaching use than its drawings suggest. A cheap indicator may help, but the evidence for it here is weak, and it should be tried properly through a whole winter before the estate buys any. School-level results were sent to the six head teachers in July, ahead of this chapter, as agreed when they joined.

## Appendix 5.A Logger checks at retrieval

On collection every logger was again exposed to the 1,000 ppm reference gas. A logger passed if it read within 75 ppm of the reference. All but two of the 36 loggers passed; among those that passed, the median deviation was 23 ppm and the largest 49 ppm. Two loggers failed, one in School E reading 96 ppm high and one in School F reading 88 ppm high. For each of these the readings were compared with the neighbouring classroom's logger to find when the two began to part, and the days after that point were removed: twelve school days for the logger in School E and eleven for the one in School F. Those removals are included in the count of valid classroom-days in section 5.3.

The classroom strand was approved by the Institute's research ethics committee on 4 December 2025 (reference KIT-REC-2025-117). texts.SEM-REF-DATA-DICTIONARY:
# Brackenfirth datasets: data dictionary

Halvard Laboratory for Building Analytics, Kestrelmoor Institute of Technology

Revision 4, released 16 September 2026. Maintained by Odalys Brennecke. Send corrections to her; do not edit the files to match what you think they should say.

## 1 What this covers

Two datasets live on the project share and are described here because they use the same building codes and the same time conventions:

- the **trend logs** exported from the Brackenfirth estate's building management system (BMS) for its air-handling units;
- the **classroom logger files** from the carbon dioxide study of spring term 2026.

This document describes file names, columns, units, flags and known quirks. It does not say how many units or classrooms there are, which were left out of an analysis, or what any analysis found. Those things are in the papers and thesis chapters that use the data, and they are the authority for them.

## 2 Building codes

Every building of the estate has a code of the form `BF-nn`, taken from the council's asset register. The code is the first part of every trend-log file name and is the `building` column of every table. The table below lists only the codes that occur in the classroom logger files. The codes of the other buildings are in the council's asset register extract (`estate_assets.xlsx`) and are not reproduced here.

| Code | School | Note for anyone working with the files |
|---|---|---|
| BF-02 | Dunnock Lea Primary | Main block and a later extension; the extension's rooms are numbered from 6 |
| BF-05 | Aldergate Primary | The annexe across the playground has no ducted supply |
| BF-09 | Tessel Lane Primary | The upper-school wing has no ducted supply |
| BF-11 | Pennystone Road Primary | Two temporary classrooms in the yard, called Hut 1 and Hut 2 on site |
| BF-12 | Larchfold Infants | Single storey; every teaching room is on the ducted supply |
| BF-14 | Marrowby Infants | Trend points carry a legacy prefix, see section 4.5 |

The thesis chapter on classroom carbon dioxide refers to these six schools by letter. The letters are not in this dictionary: they are the `school_label` column of the logger register (`classroom_co2_logger_register.csv`), next to the building code.

## 3 Time

**Trend logs.** The BMS outstations write local civil time. The export script keeps that as `ts_local` and adds `ts_utc`. On the spring clock change one hour of `ts_local` does not exist, and on the autumn change one hour occurs twice; the repeated rows can only be told apart by `ts_utc`. Always sort and join on `ts_utc`. A row describes the interval that starts at its timestamp.

**Classroom logger files.** The loggers keep UTC internally and the files have `ts_utc` only. Each logger's clock was set from a laptop at installation and compared with the laptop again at retrieval; the largest difference found was 40 seconds, and no correction has been applied.

**School calendar.** The file `school_days.csv` has one row per date with a flag for school day, holiday or staff training day. Term dates differ slightly between schools in the summer term only.

## 4 Files of the trend logs

### 4.1 Names and layout

One file per unit per calendar month, named `<building>_<unit>_<yyyy>-<mm>.csv`, for example `BF-09_AHU03_2025-11.csv`. Files are comma-separated UTF-8 with one header row. Units are numbered within a building in the order of the BMS graphics pages, which is not the order of the plant rooms.

### 4.2 Columns

`ts_utc`, `ts_local`, `building`, `unit`, then one column per logged point, then the quality flag `q`. Point columns are numeric. An empty cell means the outstation returned nothing for that point in that interval.

### 4.3 Points read by the laboratory's models

The table lists the points that the thermal-balance fit and the detectors read directly. The files also hold status bits, setpoints and the vendor's own alarm points; those keep the vendor's names and are described in the vendor's point schedule, not here.

| Column | Meaning | Unit | Sensor or source | Installer's stated accuracy | Valid range |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `t_oa` | Outdoor-air temperature | °C | Thermistor in the intake louvre | ±0.5 °C | −20 to 40 |
| `t_ra` | Return-air temperature | °C | Duct thermistor | ±0.3 °C | 5 to 35 |
| `t_ma` | Mixed-air temperature | °C | Averaging element across the mixing box | ±0.4 °C | −5 to 35 |
| `t_sa` | Supply-air temperature | °C | Duct thermistor downstream of the fan | ±0.2 °C | 5 to 45 |
| `t_hwf` | Heating water flow temperature | °C | Strap-on sensor on the flow pipe | ±1.0 °C | 10 to 90 |
| `dp_fan` | Pressure rise across the supply fan | Pa | Differential pressure transmitter | ±2% of span | 0 to 1,250 |
| `dp_fil` | Pressure drop across the filter bank | Pa | Differential pressure transmitter | ±3% of span | 0 to 500 |
| `pos_oad` | Outdoor-air damper command | fraction open | Controller output | not a measurement | 0 to 1 |
| `pos_hv` | Heating valve command | fraction open | Controller output | not a measurement | 0 to 1 |
| `spd_fan` | Supply fan speed command | fraction of full speed | Controller output | not a measurement | 0 to 1 |
| `occ` | Occupancy schedule | 0 or 1 | Time schedule in the controller | not a measurement | 0 or 1 |

The accuracies are the figures on the installer's commissioning sheets. The laboratory has not checked any of these sensors against a reference instrument, and the figures should be quoted as the installer's and not as ours. The mixed-air sensor is an averaging element strung across the mixing box: it smooths the stratification there, but it cannot be taken out and checked in a bath like a duct thermistor.

The three command columns are what the controller asked for, not what the actuator did. There is no position feedback on dampers or valves anywhere in the estate.

### 4.4 Quality flag `q`

One flag per row.

| `q` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | Good |
| 1 | One or more points in the row were filled by interpolation across a short gap |
| 2 | Outstation offline: the row is present so that the file has no holes, but its points are empty |
| 3 | Unit scheduled off (holiday or shutdown calendar) |
| 4 | A manual override was active on one of the command points |
| 5 | One or more points outside the valid range of section 4.3; the value is kept, not clipped |

Where two conditions apply, the higher number is written.

### 4.5 Known quirks

- **Legacy prefix at BF-14.** Points at Marrowby Infants are exported with the prefix `MI_` and older point names. The export script renames them to the columns above using `legacy_tags.csv`. If a column is missing for that building, look there first.
- **Duplicate rows after an outstation restart.** A restart can replay the last few intervals. Remove duplicates on `ts_utc` and `unit`, keeping the last row written.
- **Heating water sensors.** The strap-on sensors behind `t_hwf` read low where pipe lagging is missing. Treat the column as indicative; it is not used in any balance.
- **Fan pressure span.** The valid range for `dp_fan` in the table is the span of the transmitters on belt-driven fans. Transmitters on direct-drive fans have a span of 0 to 800 Pa, and the stated accuracy is a percentage of whichever span applies.
- **One outdoor sensor per building.** A building with a single intake louvre sensor writes the same `t_oa` value into the files of every unit in that building. It is one sensor repeated, not several sensors that happen to agree.
- **Occupancy schedule.** `occ` is the controller's time schedule, not a measurement of whether anyone is in the building. Evening lettings are entered by the site manager and are often missing from it.
- **Rounding.** Temperatures are stored to one decimal place, pressures to the nearest pascal, commands to two decimal places.

## 5 Files of the classroom loggers

### 5.1 Names and layout

One file per logger for the whole term, named `CO2_<logger id>.csv`, for example `CO2_Q2-2271.csv`. Comma-separated UTF-8, one header row.

### 5.2 Columns

| Column | Meaning | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| `ts_utc` | Time of the reading | UTC |
| `co2_ppm` | Carbon dioxide concentration | ppm, whole numbers |
| `temp_c` | Air temperature at the logger | °C, one decimal place |
| `rh_pct` | Relative humidity at the logger | %, whole numbers |
| `q` | Quality flag | see below |

The files hold one reading every 5 minutes.

The flag `q` in these files is not the trend-log flag. Here 0 is good; 1 marks readings taken while the logger was moved or unplugged, as recorded in the register notes; 2 marks readings removed after the check at retrieval.

### 5.3 What is not in these files

The files do not say which room or school a logger was in. Join to the logger register on the logger id. The register also holds each room's ventilation type, floor area and the dates of installation and retrieval.

### 5.4 Derived table

`classroom_days.csv` has one row per logger per school day: the mean concentration in teaching hours, the share of teaching-hours readings above 1,500 ppm, and a flag for whether the day counts as valid. It is rebuilt from the logger files by `build_classroom_days.py` and should never be edited by hand.

## 6 Revision history

- Revision 1, 14 March 2025: first issue, trend logs only.
- Revision 2, 3 October 2025: `ts_utc` added to every trend file and section 3 rewritten.
- Revision 3, 19 February 2026: quality flag 5 introduced; valid ranges added to the point table.
- Revision 4, 16 September 2026: section 2 (building codes) and section 5 (classroom logger files) added.

# Brindlewatch Account Verification Standard

Version 4.2 | Effective 15 June 2026
Owner: Odalys Ferreira-Novak, Director of Customer Care | Approved by: Trust & Security Desk
Applies to: every Customer Care agent on phone, chat and e-mail, at every tier

This Standard replaces all earlier caller-verification guidance, including section 2 of the Support Policy Handbook.

## 1. Why we verify

A Brindlewatch account controls cameras in and around someone's home. Letting the wrong person into it is the most serious mistake a Customer Care agent can make, and a sympathetic story is the usual way it happens. Verify first, help second, and treat the rules below as fixed however reasonable the caller sounds.

## 2. Standard verification

Before discussing anything specific to an account, the caller must correctly give 3 of the 5 identifiers below.

| Identifier | Notes |
|---|---|
| Full name on the account | As it is spelled on the account |
| Login e-mail address | The caller says it; the agent never reads it out or completes it |
| Billing postal code | |
| Last four digits of the payment card on file | Never ask for the full number, the expiry date or the security code |
| Serial number of a registered camera | On the label under the stand; begins with BW |

Never ask for a password.

A caller who gets an identifier wrong may try once more. After 2 failed attempts in the same contact, stop: the account is locked for phone and chat verification for 24 hours and the caller is pointed to Identity Review (section 5). Do not say which answer was wrong.

## 3. Step-up verification

Some actions need more than section 2. For these the agent sends a 6-digit one-time code to the phone number or e-mail address on file. The customer reads it back, and it expires after 10 minutes.

Step-up is required before:

- changing the login e-mail address;
- adding or removing an Authorised Contact;
- filing a recordings Deletion Request;
- changing the delivery address on an open order;
- closing the account.

## 4. Third-party callers

Only two kinds of people may be helped with an account: the account holder, and an Authorised Contact the account holder has registered. Everyone else is a third party - spouses, partners, children, parents, housemates, landlords and installers included - however much they know about the account and whether or not they live at the billing address.

With a third party, give general product and policy information only. Do not confirm whether an account exists, and do not act on one. Invite them to have the account holder call, or to be registered as an Authorised Contact.

Authorised Contacts. An account can have up to 2 Authorised Contacts. The account holder adds one in the app (Settings > Account > Authorised Contacts) or on a verified call after a step-up code. Each Authorised Contact chooses a 4-digit contact PIN and is verified by their own name plus that PIN.

| An Authorised Contact may | An Authorised Contact may not |
|---|---|
| Get troubleshooting help for the cameras | Change the login e-mail address or password, or receive a reset link |
| Check order status and billing status | Change the payment method |
| Ask for a carrier trace on an order | Delete recordings, request a refund or close the account |

Power of attorney, guardianship and the accounts of customers who have died are handled by Tier 2 Account Integrity, on documents. Tier 1 takes the caller's details and makes no change.

## 5. Customer cannot reach the e-mail on file

Verify with 3 of the 5 identifiers as usual, then send the step-up code by text message to the phone number on file. Once the code is confirmed, the customer can change the login e-mail in the app, or the agent can change it for them.

If there is no phone number on file either, start Identity Review (form IR-7). The customer uploads government photo ID and either proof of purchase or a photo of a camera's serial label. Tier 2 Account Integrity decides; tell the customer to allow up to 5 business days. A Tier 1 agent never changes a login e-mail without a confirmed step-up code or an approved IR-7.

## 6. Accessibility accommodations

Customers who are deaf or hard of hearing, or who have a speech, cognitive or motor disability, are verified to the same standard by a route that works for them.

Relay calls. A call placed through a telephone relay service or a video relay interpreter is the customer speaking. Do not ask the relay operator to verify themselves, allow extra time, and do not end the call because of silence.

Assisted calls. The account holder may have a helper - a relative, friend or carer - speak for them, provided the account holder is present and consents. Consent can be given by voice, or by replying YES to the consent message we send to the phone or e-mail on file. The helper may relay the account holder's identifiers. Consent covers that call only.

Changing channel. Any customer may ask to continue by live chat, or by e-mail to the address on file; offer this without being asked when hearing is the difficulty. One-time codes can be sent by text message instead of a voice call.

Where things are sent. An accommodation changes how we communicate, never where credentials go. Reset links, one-time codes and security notices are sent only to the contact details on file, including during an assisted call, and never to a helper's e-mail address or phone.

A helper who needs lasting access should be set up properly: as an Authorised Contact (section 4), or through a Shared Access invitation sent from the account holder's app, which gives view-only access to chosen cameras.

Longer appointments. Customers who need more time can book a 45-minute accessibility appointment, offered on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons.

## 7. Business accounts

A Brindlewatch for Business account is verified through the administrator named on it, using the same identifiers. Employees of the business who are not the administrator are third parties.

## 8. Ticket notes

Record which identifiers were used ("name, postal code, card"), never their values. Record whether a step-up code was confirmed and, on an assisted call, who the helper was and how consent was given.

## Revision history

| Version | Date | Change |
|---|---|---|
| 4.2 | 15 June 2026 | Third-party rule tightened; contact PIN introduced; destination rule for accommodations stated |
| 4.1 | 12 January 2026 | Relay-call guidance added |
| 4.0 | 1 September 2025 | Number of identifiers raised; step-up codes introduced |

# Brindlewatch Refund and Cancellation Policy

Version 3.1 | Effective 1 July 2026
Owner: Marisol Etxeberria, Billing Operations Lead | Approved by: Odalys Ferreira-Novak, Director of Customer Care

## 1. What this policy covers

This policy applies to cameras and Keep subscriptions bought directly from Brindlewatch, on our web store or billed by Brindlewatch in the app. Two kinds of purchase are outside it:

- Subscriptions billed through a phone's app store. We cannot see or reverse those charges; the customer has to ask the app store for the refund.
- Cameras bought from a retail partner. They go back to the retailer under the retailer's own return rules.

## 2. Subscription refunds

| Billing | Rule |
|---|---|
| Annual plan, first purchase or renewal | Full refund if the customer asks within 30 days of the charge date. After that window there is no refund for the unused part of the term; the plan stays active until the term ends and auto-renew can be switched off at any time. |
| Monthly plan | No refund for a partial month. Cancelling stops the next charge and the plan runs to the end of the paid month. One exception: a monthly renewal charge is refunded in full if the customer cancels within 48 hours of that charge. |

Renewal reminders. Annual plans renew automatically. We e-mail a reminder 21 days before the renewal date and again 3 days before. Not seeing a reminder does not extend the refund window.

Moving to a cheaper plan during an annual term. The customer receives a credit for each full unused month: (old annual price - new annual price) / 12 x full months remaining. It is added as account credit against future charges and is not paid back to the card. Moving to a dearer plan is covered in the Billing Guide.

Gift subscriptions cannot be refunded once the recipient has activated them.

## 3. Camera returns

A camera bought directly from us can be returned for any reason within 60 days of the delivery date. We refund the price of the item. The original shipping charge is refunded only when the camera is defective. A return label is free for a defective camera; otherwise $8 is deducted from the refund for the label.

If a subscription was bought in the same order as a camera that is returned in time, the subscription is refunded in full as well.

After the return period there is no refund. Cameras carry a 2-year limited warranty against defects, under which we repair or replace.

## 4. Where the money goes

A refund goes back to the original payment method and nowhere else - not to a different card, a bank account, a gift card or another person. If the original card has since been closed or replaced, the card issuer normally forwards the refund to the customer's new card or account. If the issuer returns the money to us, Billing Operations (Tier 2) arranges a cheque or account credit.

## 5. How long it takes

| Payment method | Time after approval |
|---|---|
| Credit or debit card | 5 to 7 business days |
| Digital wallet | up to 3 business days |
| Direct bank debit | up to 10 business days |
| Account credit | same day |

## 6. Exceptions

A refund outside sections 2 and 3 is possible only in the cases below, and each needs a supervisor's approval whatever the amount:

- The customer was charged after a cancellation we had already confirmed, and has the cancellation e-mail or reference.
- The account holder has died: refund of the full unused months of the current term.
- A defective camera left the subscription unusable while the customer waited for our replacement: refund of the months affected.
- A billing error on our side that Billing Operations has documented.

Forgetting to cancel, not using the service, moving home or switching to another brand are not exceptions.

A duplicate charge - same plan, same amount, same day - is a correction rather than a refund. A Tier 1 agent reverses it on the spot, whatever the amount.

## 7. Who may approve

| Role | May approve |
|---|---|
| Tier 1 agent | Refunds that sections 2 and 3 plainly allow, up to $150 per request |
| Supervisor (Team Lead) | Refunds above $150 and up to $500; every section 6 exception |
| Billing Operations manager | Refunds above $500; any refund by cheque |

When a refund needs a supervisor, the Tier 1 agent submits it and tells the customer three things: that it has been submitted, that a supervisor decides, and that the decision arrives by e-mail within 2 business days. The agent does not say or imply that it will be approved.

## 8. Chargebacks

If the customer has already disputed the charge with their bank, do not refund it as well. Add a note and route the ticket to Billing Operations.

## 9. Tax

Sales tax collected on a refunded amount is refunded with it.

## 2. Delivery dates are estimates

We do not guarantee a delivery date on any method. Agents quote the estimated range and do not promise a particular day, even when the tracking page shows an expected date.

There is one remedy for lateness: if a Next Business Day order arrives late, its $29.00 shipping charge is refunded automatically. Standard and Expedited orders that run late are not compensated.

## 3. Tracking says delivered, customer has nothing

1. Confirm the delivery address on the order with the customer.
2. Ask them to check with others in the household, with neighbours, with a building office or mail room, and around side doors and garages.
3. Wait 48 hours from the delivered scan. Carriers sometimes scan a parcel as delivered before it is actually dropped off.
4. If it has still not turned up after those 48 hours, a Tier 1 agent opens a carrier trace. The customer must report the problem within 14 calendar days of the delivered scan; later reports go to a supervisor.
5. A trace takes up to 6 business days. We e-mail the customer when the carrier answers.
6. If the trace does not find the parcel, the customer chooses: a replacement sent Expedited at no charge, or a refund to the original payment method. A Tier 1 agent may approve this for orders up to $300; above that a supervisor approves.

No replacement or refund is issued before the trace closes.

A second delivered-but-missing claim on the same account within 12 months is passed to Tier 2 Order Integrity, and any replacement is sent with signature required.

## 4. Lost in transit

This is a different case: there is no delivered scan. If tracking shows no movement for 5 business days (10 business days for Canada), treat the parcel as lost. A Tier 1 agent sends a replacement straight away; no trace is needed.

## 5. Who is responsible

Brindlewatch carries the risk until the carrier records delivery at the address the customer gave us.

- Wrong or incomplete address entered by the customer. If the parcel comes back to our warehouse, we send it again for a $6.95 reshipping fee. If it was delivered to the address as entered, it is the customer's responsibility and no free replacement is sent.
- Freight forwarders and parcel-receiving services. Our responsibility ends when the parcel is delivered to the forwarder.
- Orders over $400 are sent with signature required.

## 6. Damaged on arrival

Damage must be reported within 7 calendar days of delivery, with photos of the box and of the item. We send a replacement and a prepaid label for the damaged one.

## 7. Changing the address

After step-up verification, the delivery address can be changed until the order status shows Label created. From then on the customer has to use the carrier's own redirect service; we cannot change it.

## 8. Order status wording

| Status | What it means |
|---|---|
| Received | Payment taken, not yet picked |
| Label created | Packed; the carrier has been notified |
| In transit | Scanned by the carrier at least once |
| Out for delivery | On the vehicle for that day's round |
| Delivered | The carrier recorded a delivered scan |

# Password and Account Recovery Procedure

Version 2.3 | Effective 20 April 2026
Owner: Bartholomew Nkemelu-Strand, Trust & Security Desk

## 1. Password resets

Agents cannot see, read out or set a customer's password. What an agent can do is trigger a reset e-mail from the support console; the customer can do the same with Forgot password on the sign-in screen.

- The link goes to the login e-mail address on file. Any exception to that is set by the Account Verification Standard, not by this procedure.
- The link expires 30 minutes after it is sent.
- The e-mail can take up to 5 minutes to arrive. Ask the customer to look in junk and promotions folders before sending another.
- No more than 5 reset e-mails can be sent to one account in 24 hours.

## 2. Customer cannot get into the e-mail on file

After standard verification, send a one-time code by text message to the phone number on file. With the code confirmed, the login e-mail can be changed to an address the customer uses now, and the reset is sent there.

With no phone number on file, the route is Identity Review (form IR-7), handled by Tier 2 Account Integrity. Tell the customer to allow up to 3 business days.

## 3. Two-step sign-in

Customers who turned on two-step sign-in were given 10 backup codes, each usable once. A customer who has lost the authenticator device and has no backup codes left goes through Identity Review. Agents cannot switch two-step sign-in off.

## 4. Lockouts

After 6 failed sign-in attempts the account locks for 15 minutes. Agents cannot lift the lock. Ask the customer to wait it out and then use a reset rather than guessing again.

## 5. Login e-mail changed without the customer's knowledge

Treat this as a possible account takeover.

What Tier 1 does: do not change the e-mail back, do not send a reset to either address, and do not remove devices. Escalate at once to the Trust & Security desk as Priority 1.

What Security does: freezes the account - signs out every session and pauses Shared Access - and then restores it to its rightful owner.

Two protections are already in place, and it helps to tell the customer about them:

- When a login e-mail is changed, the previous address receives a notice containing a "This wasn't me" link. The link works for 7 days and reverses the change immediately.
- For 72 hours after any change of login e-mail, sensitive actions are blocked: deleting recordings, removing cameras and changing the payment method.

## 6. New-device alerts

A sign-in from a phone, tablet or browser we have not seen before sends an alert e-mail to the account holder. The customer can review everything signed in under Settings > Account > Devices and use Sign out everywhere. An alert on its own is not an incident; an alert the customer cannot explain is, and goes to the Trust & Security desk.

## 7. Shared Access

The account holder can invite up to 4 guests to view chosen cameras. A guest can watch live view and clips but cannot change settings, delete anything or see billing. Each guest signs in with their own e-mail and password, and the account holder can withdraw an invitation at any time.

## 8. What to note on the ticket

Which route was used (reset e-mail, text code, Identity Review), the time the reset was triggered, and whether the customer confirmed they were signed in before the call ended.
texts.CC-REF-PRIVACY-2026:
# Brindlewatch Privacy and Camera Access Policy

Version 5.0 | Effective 1 March 2026
Policy owner: Thaddeus Okonkwo-Reyes, Privacy Officer | Signed off by the Executive Committee on 18 February 2026

## 1. The principle

The cameras are the customer's eyes, not ours. Brindlewatch runs the service that carries and stores video; it does not watch it. This policy sets out exactly who can see what, and Customer Care agents should be able to explain it plainly when a customer asks.

## 2. Live view

No Brindlewatch employee or contractor, at any tier, can watch a customer's live view. There is no internal tool that opens a live stream. The stream is encrypted between the camera and the devices signed in to the customer's account.

## 3. Recordings

Recorded clips are stored encrypted. Tier 1 agents cannot open, play or download a clip, and the support console shows no video, no still images and no audio.

There are only two situations in which a member of staff can see a recording:

1. The customer shares it. Using Share with Support in the app, the customer picks one clip. That single clip can then be viewed for 72 hours, and only by the Tier 2 Device Diagnostics engineer assigned to the ticket. Every viewing is logged, and the customer can withdraw the share in the app at any moment.
2. The law requires it. See section 6.

What agents do see: whether each camera is online, when it was last online, its firmware version, the plan on the account and how many motion events were recorded each day.

## 4. How long clips are kept

| Plan | Clips kept for |
|---|---|
| Keep Basic | 14 days |
| Keep Plus | 30 days |
| Keep Pro | 60 days |

After that a clip is deleted automatically. Cancelling a plan does not delete the clips already recorded; each one stays until its own retention period runs out. Customers can download any clip to their phone before then.

## 5. Deleting recordings

Customers delete their own recordings. In the app: Settings > Privacy > Delete all recordings, or single clips from the timeline. The app asks for the account password first.

What happens then: the clips disappear from the account immediately, are erased from primary storage within 24 hours and from backups within 30 days. Deletion cannot be undone.

Agents cannot delete recordings from the support console. If the customer cannot use the app, the Tier 1 agent completes step-up verification and files a Deletion Request (form DR-2). The Privacy Office carries it out within 4 business days and confirms by e-mail.

Erasing an entire account - all personal data, not only video - is a separate request to the Privacy Office and is completed within 30 calendar days.

Recordings under a legal preservation order are held until the order ends. Tier 1 agents are not told which accounts these are, and refer such enquiries to the Privacy Office.

## 6. Police, courts and lawyers

Every request from police, a government body, a court or a lawyer is handled by the Legal Response team and by nobody else: legalresponse@brindlewatch.example. A Tier 1 agent who receives such a call does not confirm whether the person named has an account, shares nothing, gives the Legal Response address and logs the call.

Recordings are handed over only in response to a search warrant or court order. A subpoena obtains basic account details only, never video.

Emergencies. Where there is imminent danger of death or serious physical injury, Legal Response may disclose without a court order. Only Legal Response makes that decision; the team can be reached around the clock.

We tell the account holder before disclosing, unless the law forbids it.

A customer who wants the police to have their own footage can download the clips and hand them over themselves.

## 7. Other commitments

- Sound recording is off by default on Eave Cam and can be switched on by the customer.
- Familiar Faces, which recognises regular visitors, is opt-in; the customer can erase its data at any time.
- We do not sell customer data or video.
- Everyone at Brindlewatch with access to customer systems completes privacy training every year.

## 8. Changes to this policy

Material changes are announced to customers by e-mail at least 30 days before they take effect. Version 5.0 added Share with Support and set out the deletion timings in section 5.
texts.CC-REF-ESCALATION-2026:
# Customer Care Escalation Matrix

Version 6 | Effective 10 August 2026
Owner: Odalys Ferreira-Novak, Director of Customer Care
Read with: Account Verification Standard, Refund and Cancellation Policy, Outage and Troubleshooting Guide

## 1. What Tier 1 owns

Tier 1 agents take every first contact. They verify the caller, answer plan and billing enquiries, change plans, approve refunds within their limit, check order status, open carrier traces and work through the six troubleshooting steps. Most contacts should end at Tier 1. Escalate when a rule below says so, not because a call is difficult.

## 2. Tier 2

Tier 2 is four specialist desks.

| Desk | Send it here when |
|---|---|
| Device Diagnostics | All six troubleshooting steps are done and the fault remains; the camera's light is solid red; or this is the customer's third contact about the same fault within 14 days, even if the steps were not all repeated on this call |
| Account Integrity | Identity Review (form IR-7); power of attorney or guardianship; an account holder who has died |
| Billing Operations | A refund that cannot reach the original payment method; a chargeback; an invoice error; a travel-charge dispute beyond the first-trip courtesy |
| Order Integrity | A second delivered-but-missing claim on the account within 12 months; suspected reselling or fraud on an order |

Handing over. Use a warm transfer when Tier 2 is staffed: Monday to Saturday, 8:00 am to 8:00 pm Central. Outside those hours open a ticket; Tier 2 makes first contact within 1 business day. Before handing over, write up what the customer reported and the steps already done, plus firmware version and light colour for a device fault.

## 3. Engineering

Tier 1 never contacts Engineering. Only Tier 2 opens an Engineering case, and only when a defect has been reproduced on 5 or more accounts on the same firmware version, or when recordings have been lost. Engineering has no customer-facing response target: do not quote a fix date or a firmware release date, even if a colleague mentions one.

## 4. Trust & Security desk

Security cases go straight from Tier 1 to the Trust & Security desk and are not routed through Tier 2. The desk is staffed 24 hours a day, every day, and every case is Priority 1.

Escalate at once when:

- the customer believes someone else has been in their account or watching their cameras;
- the login e-mail was changed and the customer did not do it;
- an unfamiliar voice has come through a camera's speaker;
- a device the customer does not recognise appears in the Devices list;
- the customer says they are in danger from someone who has, or used to have, access to the cameras;
- anyone reports a security weakness in our products.

Warm transfer and stay on the line until Security answers. If nobody answers within 10 minutes, open a Priority 1 ticket and tell the customer that Security will call back within 1 hour. Do not troubleshoot, reset passwords or remove devices yourself in these cases.

## 5. Supervisor (Team Lead)

- The customer asks for a supervisor. Never refuse. If none is free, a supervisor calls back within 4 business hours.
- A refund above the Tier 1 approval limit, or any refund exception.
- A goodwill credit above $25. A Tier 1 agent may give a goodwill credit of up to $25, once per account in any 3 months.
- The customer threatens legal action or says they will go to the press. The supervisor informs Legal Response.
- A caller who remains abusive after 2 warnings.

## 6. Privacy Office and Legal Response

Deletion requests and requests for a copy of personal data go to the Privacy Office through the forms named in the Privacy and Camera Access Policy. Anything from police, courts or lawyers goes to Legal Response and is never handled on the call.

## 7. What to tell the customer

Give the ticket number, the name of the team that now has it, and that team's response target. Do not promise an outcome, and do not promise when the matter will be resolved: a response target is when the team first responds, not when the problem is fixed.

| Team | Response target |
|---|---|
| Tier 2 desks | first contact within 1 business day |
| Trust & Security desk | within 1 hour, any day |
| Supervisor callback | within 4 business hours |
| Engineering | none given to customers |

## 8. Bouncing

A ticket sent to the wrong desk costs the customer a day. If unsure which Tier 2 desk applies, ask in the Tier 2 duty channel before transferring. A desk that receives a ticket in error reroutes it itself and does not send it back to Tier 1.

# Brindlewatch Billing Guide and Roam Link Rates

Version 2.4 | Effective 1 February 2026 | Owner: Billing Operations
All prices in US dollars, before sales tax

## 1. Keep plans

| Plan | Monthly billing | Annual billing | Cameras | Clip history |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Keep Basic | $6 per month | $60 per year | 1 | 14 days |
| Keep Plus | $13 per month | $130 per year | up to 5 | 30 days |
| Keep Pro | $22 per month | $220 per year | up to 20 | 60 days, plus continuous recording |

Without a plan a camera still gives live view and alerts, but nothing is recorded.

## 2. Billing dates

A monthly plan bills on the same day of each month as the day it started; if a month has no such day, it bills on the last day of that month. An annual plan bills once a year on its start date. Every charge produces an invoice, e-mailed to the login address and listed in the app under Settings > Billing.

## 3. Changing plan mid-month

Moving up on a monthly plan takes effect at once. We charge the difference for the days left: (new monthly price - old monthly price) x days remaining / 30. Every month is treated as 30 days for this purpose.

Example: Keep Basic to Keep Pro with 15 days left is (22 - 6) x 15 / 30 = $8.00 charged today, then $22 from the next billing date.

Moving down on a monthly plan takes effect on the next billing date, with no credit for the current month.

## 4. Roam Link

Roam Link is the cellular service for Trek Cam. It costs $5 per camera per month and covers the United States. Each camera includes 3 GB of data per month, and allowances are not shared between cameras. Extra data is $4 per GB, and a part GB is rounded up to a whole one.

Example: a Trek Cam uses 4.2 GB in a month. It is 1.2 GB over, billed as 2 GB: $8 on top of the monthly fee.

## 5. Using a Trek Cam abroad

Outside the United States a Trek Cam on Roam Link connects through partner networks, and each day abroad carries a Roam Day fee.

| Zone | Countries | Roam Day fee | Cap per camera per billing cycle | Roam Week pass |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Zone 1 | Canada, Mexico | $10 per camera per day | $60 | $45 per camera |
| Zone 2 | United Kingdom, Ireland, European Union | $15 per camera per day | $90 | $70 per camera |

Roam Link does not work in other countries.

How days are counted:

- A day is a calendar day, midnight to midnight in the account's home time zone - not a 24-hour period from the first connection.
- Any connection to a partner network on a day, however short, makes that day a Roam Day.
- Each Trek Cam is charged separately.
- A camera that is switched off, or set to Wi-Fi only, does not connect and is not charged.
- Data used abroad comes out of the same monthly allowance.

Cap. Roam Day fees stop adding up once they reach the cap for that camera in a billing cycle. The cap counts Roam Day fees only.

Roam Week pass. A pass covers one camera for 7 consecutive calendar days from activation. It has to be activated in the app before the camera first connects abroad and cannot be added to a trip afterwards. Days abroad outside those 7 days are charged as Roam Days.

Examples:

- One camera crosses into Canada at 11:10 pm on the 3rd and comes back at 7:30 am on the 5th. The trip lasted about 32 hours but touched three calendar days: 3 x $10 = $30.
- Three cameras spend 3 calendar days in Ireland: 3 x 3 x $15 = $135.
- One camera spends 9 calendar days in Mexico: 9 x $10 would be more than the Zone 1 cap, so the cap amount is billed.

On the invoice these lines read ROAM DAY Z1 or ROAM DAY Z2, and the quantity is camera-days.

## 6. When a customer disputes travel charges

A Roam Day charge is correct when the connection log shows the camera on a partner network that day. Tier 1 agents see the camera-day count on the invoice but not the log.

First-trip courtesy. If the invoice is the first on the account ever to carry Roam Day fees, a Tier 1 agent may credit up to $30 of them, once per account. Any larger adjustment, or a second request, goes to Billing Operations (Tier 2), who review the connection log. Do not tell the customer what Billing Operations will decide.

## 7. Failed payments

If a charge fails we retry it 3, 6 and 10 days after the failed charge. If the day-10 retry also fails, the plan is suspended. Live view keeps working; clips already recorded are kept for 30 days after suspension and then deleted. Paying the balance within that time restores the plan and the clips.

## 8. Tax and currency

Sales tax is added at the rate for the billing postal code. Customers in Canada are billed in US dollars; their card issuer sets the exchange rate and any foreign-transaction fee.
texts.CC-REF-TROUBLESHOOTING-2026:
# Outage and Troubleshooting Guide

Revised 1 September 2026 | Maintained by Tier 2 Device Diagnostics (Ezekiel Brandvold-Osei) | For Tier 1 agents

## Before anything else: is it us?

Open the Incident Board before touching the customer's setup.

| Level | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Severity 1 | Live view or recording is unavailable for more than 10% of cameras in a region |
| Severity 2 | The service works but is degraded: late notifications, slow clip loading |

While an incident is open for the customer's region, do not walk them through device steps, and never have them factory-reset a camera. Say that there is a known incident and that their equipment is not at fault. Give a time for the fix only if the Incident Board shows one; never estimate one yourself. Customers can follow updates at status.brindlewatch.example.

Outage credit. When a Severity 1 incident lasts more than 24 hours in a row, affected subscribers are credited 10% of their monthly plan fee for each full 24 hours, up to a maximum of 50%. Annual subscribers get the same percentages of one-twelfth of the annual price. The credit is applied automatically on the next invoice; customers do not need to ask and agents do not add it by hand. Severity 2 incidents carry no credit.

## Camera offline: the six steps

Work through these in order and note each one on the ticket.

1. Read the light.

| Light | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Solid green | Online |
| Blinking blue | Pairing mode |
| Solid amber | Starting up; this can take up to 90 seconds |
| Blinking red | No network connection |
| Solid red | Hardware fault - stop here and escalate to Tier 2 Device Diagnostics |

2. Check power. Use the original adapter and try a different outlet. An Eave Cam needs its battery above 15% to reconnect.

3. Check the Wi-Fi band. Lantern Cam (2nd generation) and Eave Cam connect on 2.4 GHz only. Lantern Cam (3rd generation) uses 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz. A router set to broadcast only a 5 GHz network will not work with a 2.4 GHz camera. Trek Cam uses Wi-Fi or cellular.

4. Restart the router. Unplug it for 30 seconds, plug it back in and wait 3 minutes before checking the camera.

5. Check signal. In the app under Device Health, the signal should read -67 dBm or stronger (closer to zero). If it is weaker, move the camera or the router closer together; thick walls and metal doors are the usual cause.

6. Factory reset. Hold the reset button for 12 seconds, until the light blinks amber, then pair the camera again in the app. A factory reset clears the camera's Wi-Fi settings and activity zones. It does not delete recordings already in the cloud and does not change the plan.

If the camera is still offline after step 6, escalate to Tier 2 Device Diagnostics with the light colour, the firmware version and the steps done.

## Firmware

| Camera | Current firmware |
|---|---|
| Lantern Cam (3rd generation) | 4.8.2 |
| Lantern Cam (2nd generation) | 4.5.9 (final release) |
| Eave Cam | 3.11.0 |
| Trek Cam | 2.6.1 |

Cameras update themselves between 2:00 am and 4:00 am local time, when idle. A customer cannot force an update; leaving the camera powered and online overnight is enough.

Known fault: Eave Cam firmware 3.10.4 made night vision flicker. It is corrected in 3.11.0.

## Notifications late or missing

Check the Incident Board for a Severity 2 incident first. Then check that notifications are allowed for the app in the phone's settings, that battery saver is not restricting it, and that the app is version 7.3 or newer.

## Live view will not load although the camera is online

Ask whether the phone is on a VPN and have them switch it off. Have them change between Wi-Fi and mobile data. Reinstalling the app is the last resort and does not affect recordings.

## Trek Cam on cellular

In Device Health the SIM status should read Active and the camera should show at least two signal bars. Abroad, connections carry Roam Day fees; see the Billing Guide before advising a customer who is travelling.

## Eave Cam battery

A full charge typically lasts 4 to 6 months. Below -10 C the battery drains faster, and it will not charge below 0 C. Bring the camera indoors to charge it.

# Brindlewatch Support Policy Handbook

Owner: Ignatius Varga-Lindqvist, Support Operations Manager | Next scheduled review: March 2026

texts.CC-REF-REPAIR-2026:
# Brindlewatch Repair and Replacement Service Terms

Version 2.2 | Effective 1 September 2026
Owner: Florentyn Akabueze-Marsh, Head of Device Service | Approved by: Odalys Ferreira-Novak, Director of Customer Care
Applies to: Lantern Cam, Eave Cam and Trek Cam, and to accessories sold under the Brindlewatch name

## 1. What these terms are for

These terms describe what happens once a camera has developed a fault in use: how a claim is opened, how the unit travels, what the customer receives and what, if anything, it costs. They are the wording Customer Care relies on when a customer asks.

They do not set the length of the limited warranty, which is stated in the Refund and Cancellation Policy and printed on the product box. They also leave two neighbouring cases to other documents:

- a camera the customer simply wants to send back for their money - Refund and Cancellation Policy;
- a parcel that arrives damaged, or does not arrive - Shipping and Delivery Policy.

## 2. Who decides

A claim under these terms starts only when Tier 2 Device Diagnostics has confirmed a hardware fault and recorded a fault code. Tier 1 agents do not diagnose hardware and do not open a claim on their own judgement, however obvious the fault sounds. Once the fault code is recorded, Device Diagnostics issues the Return Authorisation and chooses the service route in section 3. Tier 1 can read the route and its progress in the support console and explain both to the customer.

Nothing in these terms changes when or how a suspected fault is passed to Device Diagnostics. That is set by the Escalation Matrix and the Outage and Troubleshooting Guide.

## 3. Service routes

| Route | When it is used | What the customer receives |
|---|---|---|
| Standard exchange | A fault inside the warranty; the default route | A replacement unit, dispatched no later than 4 business days after the faulty unit is scanned in at the service centre |
| Advance exchange | A fault inside the warranty, where the customer asks not to be left without a camera and agrees to a card hold | A replacement unit dispatched first; the faulty unit follows and must be scanned in within 20 calendar days |
| Paid repair | A fault outside the warranty, or damage that is not a defect (section 6) | The customer's own unit, repaired for the flat fee in section 7 |

A replacement unit is either new or renewed. A renewed unit is one that came back to us, was rebuilt with a new housing seal and lens cover, and passed the same bench checks as a new unit. The customer cannot choose between the two, and agents do not say which will be sent.

Every replacement unit is covered for the remainder of the original warranty or for 90 days from its delivery, whichever is longer. An exchange does not start a new warranty: the date on the proof of purchase goes on defining it.

## 4. Advance exchange

Only Device Diagnostics authorises an advance exchange. Tier 1 may tell a customer that the route exists, but not that it will be granted. It is offered once the fault code is recorded and the customer agrees to a temporary hold on a payment card.

| Camera | Hold placed on the card |
|---|---|
| Lantern Cam | $65 |
| Eave Cam | $115 |
| Trek Cam | $185 |

The hold is an authorisation, not a charge, and it is released when the faulty unit is scanned in at the service centre. The 20 calendar days run from the day the replacement is dispatched. If the faulty unit has not been scanned in by then, the hold becomes a charge and the claim is closed. A customer who sends the unit in late can ask for the charge to be returned; the Device Service desk decides, not Tier 1.

Advance exchange is not offered on a paid repair, on accessories, or to a customer who already has an advance-exchange hold open.

The replacement under an advance exchange travels by Expedited delivery at our cost. The label for the faulty unit is in the same box.

## 5. Sending the unit in

Return Authorisation. Each claim has a Return Authorisation number beginning RA- and a shipping label, both e-mailed to the customer. The number and the label stay valid for 25 calendar days from the day of issue. After that Device Diagnostics has to issue them again.

What to send. The camera only. The customer keeps the stand or mount, the power adapter and the cables; accessories sent in with a camera are not returned. Any sturdy box will do; the original packaging is not needed.

Where it goes. Units travel under the label to the service centre in Marrow Creek. Under a claim inside the warranty the label is prepaid.

Proof of purchase. For a web store order, the order number is enough. For a camera bought from a retail partner, the customer supplies the dated receipt; warranty service is the same wherever the camera was bought. Where there is neither, the manufacturing date held against the unit is used as the purchase date.

Progress e-mails. The customer is e-mailed at three points: when the unit is scanned in, when the bench result is recorded, and when the outbound parcel is dispatched.

## 6. What counts as a defect

A defect is a failure of materials or workmanship in normal use. The fault code and the bench inspection decide; the customer's description does not.

The following are not defects and go down the paid repair route, whatever the age of the camera:

- impact damage, such as a cracked housing, a cracked lens or a bent stand joint;
- liquid inside a Lantern Cam, or inside an Eave Cam or Trek Cam whose housing has been opened;
- damage caused by a power adapter or charger that is not a Brindlewatch one;
- a unit that has been opened or modified;
- cosmetic marks that do not affect how the camera works.

Weather. Eave Cam and Trek Cam are built to be used outdoors, and water found inside a housing that has never been opened is a defect. Lantern Cam is an indoor camera: fitting one outdoors, or in a bathroom or greenhouse, is not normal use.

More than one fault. Where the bench finds a defect and damage on the same unit, the damage decides the route.

## 7. Paid repair

| Camera | Flat fee |
|---|---|
| Lantern Cam (either generation) | $34 |
| Eave Cam | $52 |
| Trek Cam | $68 |

The flat fee is charged for each unit and is the same whatever the fault. It covers the inbound label, the bench work, the parts and the return of the unit by Standard delivery. If a unit cannot be repaired, a renewed unit of the same model is supplied for the same fee.

Faster return. A customer who wants a repaired unit back sooner can pay the Expedited charge set out in the Shipping and Delivery Policy. It is charged once for each return parcel, not for each unit, and units on the same Return Authorisation travel back in one parcel. Next Business Day is not offered for service returns.

The quote. After the bench inspection the customer is e-mailed a quote. No work is done until the quote has been accepted and paid. The quote stays open for 10 calendar days from the day it is sent. If it has not been accepted in that time, the unit is sent back unrepaired by Standard delivery at no charge.

Turnaround. A repaired unit is dispatched no later than 9 business days after payment. This is a target for dispatch, not a delivery date.

Payment. The fee is paid by card or digital wallet. Account credit cannot be put towards a repair fee.

Several units. Each unit on a Return Authorisation gets its own line on the quote. The customer can accept some lines and decline others; declined units come back unrepaired with the repaired ones.

## 8. Accessories

Accessories sold under the Brindlewatch name - mounts, stands, power adapters, charging cables and weather hoods - are covered against defects for 1 year from purchase. A faulty accessory is exchanged, never repaired, and the exchange is sent by Standard delivery without the old accessory having to come back. Accessories from other makers are not covered, and neither is anything they damage.

An accessory claim does not need a fault code. A Tier 1 agent raises it once the order or receipt has been seen, and the console allows 2 accessory exchanges against any one order before it asks for a Team Lead to sign off the next.

## 9. Units we cannot take in

The service centre does not open a parcel that arrives without a Return Authorisation number on the label; it goes back to the sender. Units sent from outside the United States and Canada are not accepted. A unit that arrives wet, or in packaging that is leaking, is logged by the receiving clerk, sealed and held while Device Diagnostics contacts the customer.

## 10. Customers in Canada

The routes and fees are the same, with three differences.

- The label is not prepaid. The customer pays the postage to Marrow Creek and is reimbursed against a postal receipt, up to $28 for each claim.
- Advance exchange is offered for Lantern Cam and Eave Cam only.
- Outbound parcels are sent duty paid, and the dispatch targets in sections 3 and 7 apply unchanged; delivery then takes the Canada time given in the Shipping and Delivery Policy.

## 11. After the bench inspection

The bench records one of four outcomes.

Fault confirmed. The claim continues down the route already chosen.

No fault found. The unit is sent back as it came. The first no-fault-found return of a camera is free. A second no-fault-found return of the same camera inside one year carries a $19 handling charge, which is taken before the unit is sent back.

Customer damage found on a claim inside the warranty. The claim moves to the paid repair route and a quote is issued. The inspection report, with the technician's images of the damage, is e-mailed to the customer. A customer who disagrees with the report may ask for a second inspection, and has to ask within 21 calendar days of the date on the report. The second inspection is carried out by a different technician, the quote is paused while it is pending, and its result is final. Each claim can have one second inspection.

Repeat fault. When a camera has already been exchanged twice for the same fault code, the next unit sent is new, not renewed, and the Head of Device Service reviews the case before it is dispatched.

## 12. Cover on repair work

A paid repair is covered for 180 days from the day the repaired unit is delivered. If the same fault comes back in that time, we repair the unit again at no charge, with the label prepaid in both directions. The cover applies to the fault that was repaired and to nothing else, and it neither restarts nor lengthens the limited warranty.

A unit supplied in place of one that could not be repaired (section 7) carries the same 180 days.

## 13. What agents say, and what they leave unsaid

- Say that Device Diagnostics decides whether there is a hardware fault and which route applies. Do not tell a customer that a claim, an exchange or an advance exchange will be granted.
- Quote a fee from section 7 only when the warranty position is already recorded; otherwise say that the fee applies if the camera turns out to be outside the warranty or damaged.
- Give the dispatch targets as targets. Do not turn them into a delivery day.
- Do not say whether a replacement unit will be new or renewed.
- What happens to subscription charges while a camera is away is a matter for the Refund and Cancellation Policy, not for these terms.
- A customer who is unhappy with a bench outcome is told about the second inspection where it applies. Do not offer a fee waiver; only the Device Service desk can waive a fee.

## 14. The Device Service desk

The Device Service desk is the team at the service centre that owns claims once a unit has been scanned in. Tier 1 reaches it through the claim record in the support console, by adding a note marked for the desk; the desk answers notes by the end of the next business day. Customers are not put through to the desk, and all contact with the customer about a claim goes through Customer Care or the progress e-mails.

## 15. Records

Each claim record carries the fault code, the Return Authorisation number, the route, the proof of purchase used, the bench outcome and, for a paid repair, the dates on which the quote was sent, accepted and paid. Agents add what the customer was told on each contact.

## Revision history

| 2.1 | 9 February 2026 | Advance exchange opened to Trek Cam |
